newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers battle on in flood-hit Oder.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers battle on in flood-hit Oder.

text.p: Thousands of soldiers battled tirelessly on Monday to shore up flood barriers on the swollen River Oder in eastern Germany, despite the first drop in water levels for weeks.

A local flood crisis committee spokesman said dikes protecting the Oderbruch, a large area well below river level, could still burst at any time under pressure from the river, which runs along Germany's border with Poland.

Sandbags propping up dikes nearby in Frankfurt an der Oder would be removed and sent further north to the Oderbruch basin, which is 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long and remains the most vulnerable place, he said.
Officials said six million sandbags, some flown in from France and Denmark, had been used in the spectacular operation involving 10,000 soldiers and hundreds more police, border guards and villagers.

"The Oder is falling by about three to four cm every day at the moment. But, on average, it is still four or five metres higher than its normal level," said Peter Salenders, a spokesman for the flood crisis committee in the town of Bad Freienwalde said.
Officials say the river will have to fall by at least 1.5 metres before it becomes safe for 15,000 residents to return to their homes.

"It could take several more days before we are over the worst...We are hoping for more good weather. If we have heavy rainstorms like those that swept the Czech Republic and Poland the river will rise and the dike could burst," he said.

The Oder, which has started dropping for the first time in three weeks, is freakishly swollen by the same rains that caused flooding which last month killed more than 100 people and did billions of dollars' worth of damage in the Czech Republic and Poland.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

Government ministers from Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic focused on the clean-up operation needed in the aftermath of the floods and said they would develop an action programme to minimise future flood damage.

"Our help can't end as soon as the time of the acute danger is over," said German Environment Minister Angela Merkel during a tour of the area. "The people need help and support over weeks and months."

Merkel met her Polish counterpart Stanislaw Zelichowski und deputy Czech Environment Minister Vladislav Bizek in the border town of Frankfurt an der Oder. They agreed to work together and said experts would meet to discuss concrete plans next month.
German officials said the area south of Frankfurt an der Oder had recorded the sharpest drop in water levels.
In Ratzdorf, at the confluence of the Oder and Neisse rivers, water levels had fallen 17 cm (10 inches) in the past 24 hours, a spokeswoman for the regional interior ministry said.
